MC68230 PI/T

This document defines the MC68230 parallel interface and timer, its MC68EC000 bus connection, the bit-banged monitor DDC channel, the user I/O header, and the two vectored interrupt levels it owns. Return to the main page.

1. Purpose and Scope

The MC68230 supplies two 8-bit parallel ports, four programmable handshake pins, eight dual-function port C pins, and a 24-bit timer. The board uses two port C pins as a bit-banged DDC bus to the monitor connector, routes the remaining general-purpose pins to a user header, and takes the port and timer interrupts on their own processor levels. This page fixes every motherboard connection to the device and the firmware rules that the wiring imposes.

The Memory Map owns the slot assignment. Bus and Address Decode owns IO9_n, the PIT_CS_n gate, the global completion tree, and timeout behavior. Interrupts owns the priority encoder inputs and the two acknowledge strobes, and Clock and Reset owns PIT_CLK and PERIPH_RESET_n.

The MC68230 is a native M68000 peripheral. It decodes its own register selects, drives the data bus, and produces its own /DTACK, so it needs no cycle sequencer of the kind the RTC, floppy, and VGA interfaces use. The motherboard adds one OR gate, one clock branch, and five resistors.

Signal names ending in _n, and signal names written with a leading slash, are active low. The board uses +5 V logic and through-hole packages. Every IC family selected here existed before 1994.

2. Architecture

MC68EC000 bus                    MC68230 PI/T

A5..A1 -------------------------> RS5..RS1
D7..D0 <-----------------------> D7..D0
R/W ----------------------------> R/W
IO9_n --> U_OR_DTACK gate 2 ----> /CS
LDS_n --> U_OR_DTACK gate 2
PIT_CLK ------------------------> CLK
PERIPH_RESET_n -----------------> RESET
IACK_L4_n ----------------------> PC6/PIACK
IACK_L5_n ----------------------> PC7/TIACK

PIT_DTACK_n <--- 4.7 kohm pull-up --- /DTACK
PIT_PIRQ_n  <--- 4.7 kohm pull-up --- PC5/PIRQ
PIT_TIRQ_n  <--- 4.7 kohm pull-up --- PC3/TOUT

DDC_SCL <------- 4.7 kohm pull-up --- PC0 ---> J_VGA pin 15
DDC_SDA <------- 4.7 kohm pull-up --- PC1 ---> J_VGA pin 12

PA7..PA0, PB7..PB0, H1..H4, PC2, PC4 -> J_PIT_USER
F_PIT_5V ----------------------------> J_PIT_USER +5 V pins

PIT_DTACK_n joins the motherboard completion tree at U_DTACK_B gate 1. The same net terminates register cycles, level-4 acknowledge cycles, and level-5 acknowledge cycles, because the completion tree stays active during CPU space.

PC4/DMAREQ reaches the user header as a port C pin. The board has no DMA controller, so firmware leaves the DMA request function unselected.

3. Bus Interface

MC68230 processor-bus connections
MC68230 signal Motherboard connection Function
D7..D0 CPU D7..D0 Register data and interrupt vectors.
RS1..RS5 CPU A1..A5, in order Selects one of 32 register positions.
/CS PIT_CS_n Selects the device in slot 9 on the lower byte lane during a normal bus cycle.
R/W CPU R/W High for reads and low for writes.
CLK PIT_CLK Free-running 10 MHz internal timing reference.
RESET PERIPH_RESET_n Clears the control and direction registers.
/DTACK PIT_DTACK_n Terminates register cycles and both vectored acknowledge cycles.
PC6/PIACK IACK_L4_n Port interrupt acknowledge from the level decoder.
PC7/TIACK IACK_L5_n Timer interrupt acknowledge from the level decoder.

Chip Select

The MC68230 has no separate data-strobe input, so the byte-lane strobe belongs in the chip-select equation. Gate 2 of U_OR_DTACK, a spare SN74F32N OR gate in the motherboard glue logic, combines the slot select with LDS_n. 

PIT_CS_n = IO9_n OR LDS_n

IO9_n already carries the address decode and the normal bus-cycle qualification, so PIT_CS_n satisfies the MC68230 requirement that address strobe, a data strobe, and the address bits all appear in the chip select. The gate is FAST rather than HCT because PIT_CS_n also starts the acknowledgement release path measured in section 13.

IO9_n is inactive during CPU space, so /CS stays high while PIACK or TIACK is low. The MC68230 forbids asserting /CS, PIACK, and TIACK in any combination, and the decoder structure makes that impossible.

Addressing Rules

Software accesses the PI/T as bytes at odd addresses. A lower-byte access asserts LDS_n; an upper-byte-only access leaves PIT_CS_n high and reaches the motherboard bus timeout. A word access includes the lower lane and completes, but only D7..D0 carry PI/T data, so word accesses are outside the interface contract.

Address lines A16..A6 do not enter the local decode. The 64-byte register block repeats throughout slot 9. The table in section 4 names the canonical copy beginning at $F20000.

Completion Response

The MC68230 drives /DTACK high before entering its high-impedance state, and it contains an internal active pull-up that shortens the rising edge. R_PIT_DTACK, 4.7 kohm to +5 V, holds the completion-tree input inactive while the device is not driving it. This matches the MC68901 arrangement on the same tree.

The device asserts /DTACK on a falling PIT_CLK edge after it recognizes the chip select. It never asserts /DTACK for a cycle it does not own, so an access to another slot leaves PIT_DTACK_n released.

Bus Cycle Recovery

The MC68230 recognizes a new chip select three PIT_CLK periods after the clock edge on which it asserted /DTACK for the previous cycle. A chip select that arrives inside that window does not produce an error: the device postpones the new cycle, and with it /DTACK, until its internal operations finish. The processor waits.

Three PIT_CLK periods are 300 ns. The longest postponement is far inside the 51.1 microsecond motherboard timeout, so back-to-back PI/T accesses cost wait states and nothing else. Section 13 shows that consecutive accesses do not reach the window in practice.

4. Register Map

The MC68230 answers 32 register selects. Twenty-three hold registers and the rest read as zero. The register functions and select values come from the MC68230 register model; this table does not prescribe firmware values.

Canonical MC68230 register addresses
Address RS5..RS1 Register Purpose
$F20001 00000 PGCR Port mode, handshake enables, and handshake sense.
$F20003 00001 PSRR Service-request select, interrupt pin functions, and port interrupt priority.
$F20005 00010 PADDR Port A direction; one selects output and zero selects input.
$F20007 00011 PBDDR Port B direction.
$F20009 00100 PCDDR Port C direction, including the two DDC pins.
$F2000B 00101 PIVR Port interrupt vector base; reads $0F until written.
$F2000D 00110 PACR Port A submode, H2 control, and the H1 and H2 interrupt enables.
$F2000F 00111 PBCR Port B submode, H4 control, and the H3 and H4 interrupt enables.
$F20011 01000 PADR Port A data.
$F20013 01001 PBDR Port B data.
$F20015 01010 PAAR Port A pin levels; reading does not disturb the handshake.
$F20017 01011 PBAR Port B pin levels; reading does not disturb the handshake.
$F20019 01100 PCDR Port C data; input bits return the pin level, which is how firmware reads the DDC lines.
$F2001B 01101 PSR Handshake pin levels H4..H1 and status bits H4S..H1S.
$F2001D-$F2001F 01110-01111 Null Read as zero.
$F20021 10000 TCR TOUT and TIACK function, zero-detect control, clock source, and timer enable.
$F20023 10001 TIVR Timer interrupt vector; reads $0F until written.
$F20025 10010 Null Read as zero.
$F20027 10011 CPRH Counter preload, bits 23 through 16.
$F20029 10100 CPRM Counter preload, bits 15 through 8.
$F2002B 10101 CPRL Counter preload, bits 7 through 0.
$F2002D 10110 Null Read as zero.
$F2002F 10111 CNTRH Current count, bits 23 through 16.
$F20031 11000 CNTRM Current count, bits 15 through 8.
$F20033 11001 CNTRL Current count, bits 7 through 0.
$F20035 11010 TSR Zero-detect status; firmware clears it by writing a one to bit 0.
$F20037-$F2003F 11011-11111 Null Read as zero.

The three counter registers are read as three separate bytes, so a count read while the timer runs can straddle a borrow. Firmware that needs a coherent 24-bit count reads the three bytes twice and repeats when the high byte changes.

5. Clock and Reset

The MC68230 contains dynamic logic. Its clock must run at all times. The 10 MHz grade accepts 2.0 to 10.0 MHz, a 100 to 500 ns period, and 45 to 250 ns in each half period, with rise and fall times at or below 10 ns. The clock does not need a phase relationship with the processor clock, and the device handles the resulting uncertainty through /DTACK.

PIT_CLK is a 10 MHz square wave with 50 ns in each half period, which clears the 45 ns minimum by 5 ns, and the CD74ACT244E edges are far shorter than the 10 ns limit. The 500 ns period maximum and the 250 ns half-period maximum are why the net is never gated: a stopped clock loses the device's internal state within one period of the limit.

PIT_CLK comes from U_IO_CLK_BUF, the CD74ACT244E I/O clock buffer defined in Clock and Reset. Two buffer stages separate PIT_CLK from CPU_CLK_10, so the PI/T clock lags the processor clock by the buffer delay and keeps the same 100 ns period and edge structure. The processor clock net gains one CD74ACT244E input and loses the bus-timeout counter, so its known load is unchanged.

The lag helps the chip-select setup and costs margin on the acknowledgement arrival. Section 13 works both directions.

Reset Behavior

PERIPH_RESET_n drives the MC68230 RESET input. Asserting it clears PGCR, PSRR, PACR, PBCR, the three data direction registers, TCR, and the port status bits, and it loads $0F into PIVR and TIVR.

State of the board's PI/T pins after reset
Pins State Board consequence
PA7..PA0, PB7..PB0 Inputs, internal pull-ups active The user header floats high and drives nothing.
PC0, PC1 Inputs DDC_SCL and DDC_SDA release to their 4.7 kohm pull-ups, which is the idle bus state.
PC3/TOUT, PC5/PIRQ Port C inputs; alternate functions unselected PIT_TIRQ_n and PIT_PIRQ_n stay released, so the encoder sees no request.
PC6/PIACK, PC7/TIACK Port C inputs; alternate functions unselected An acknowledge to level 4 or level 5 gets no response until firmware enables the interrupt.
H1..H4 Inputs; H2 and H4 pulled up Status bits held clear while the enables are clear.

Reset does not clear PADR, PBDR, or PCDR. Their contents after power-on are undefined, so firmware writes them before it programs any direction register. Section 11 states the ordering rule.

6. Port Assignment

Board use of every MC68230 port pin
Pins Board function Destination
PA7..PA0 Bit-programmable I/O J_PIT_USER
PB7..PB0 Bit-programmable I/O J_PIT_USER
H1, H2 Edge-sensitive status inputs for port A J_PIT_USER
H3, H4 Edge-sensitive status inputs for port B J_PIT_USER
PC0 DDC clock, driven as open drain DDC_SCL to J_VGA pin 15
PC1 DDC data, driven as open drain DDC_SDA to J_VGA pin 12
PC2/TIN Port C I/O, or an external timer clock or run/halt control if firmware selects it J_PIT_USER
PC3/TOUT Timer interrupt request PIT_TIRQ_n
PC4/DMAREQ Port C I/O; the DMA function stays unselected J_PIT_USER
PC5/PIRQ Port interrupt request PIT_PIRQ_n
PC6/PIACK Port interrupt acknowledge input IACK_L4_n
PC7/TIACK Timer interrupt acknowledge input IACK_L5_n

Both ports run in mode 0 with the bit I/O submode, so each port A and port B pin takes its direction from its own bit in PADDR or PBDDR, and the four handshake pins act as status and interrupt inputs rather than transfer controls. That fits a header whose attached hardware is not known at design time.

PC6 and PC7 carry acknowledge strobes and never reach the header. Firmware can still read their pin levels through PCDR while they carry the alternate function, which is useful during bring-up.

7. Monitor DDC Channel

PC0 and PC1 form a 5 V bus that firmware drives one bit at a time. It carries the display data channel to the monitor: PC0 is the DDC clock and PC1 is the DDC data line. The bus leaves this subsystem as DDC_SCL and DDC_SDA and connects only to the DDC pins of J_VGA, so firmware can read a monitor's EDID over DDC2B. The MC68230 has no open-drain port outputs, so the interface produces the open-drain behavior the bus requires by switching pin direction instead of pin level. 

PCDR bits 1 and 0 = 0     written once during initialization

PCDDR bit = 1  -> pin drives low, line asserted
PCDDR bit = 0  -> pin is an input, line released to its pull-up

PCDR bit read  -> the pin level, whatever drives it

Writing a one to either PCDR bit while the matching direction bit is set drives the line high and fights every other device on the bus. Firmware treats those two PCDR bits as constant zeros.

Reading PCDR returns the pin level for a pin programmed as an input, which gives firmware the acknowledge bit from the monitor and the released level of the clock line. Waiting for PC0 to read high after releasing it implements clock-stretch tolerance.

DDC channel electrical arrangement
Item Value Basis
Bus voltage +5 V DDC2B is a 5 V bus. The pull-ups on this page return to the board +5 V rail. The separate +5 V pin the monitor draws from, J_VGA pin 9, and its fuse are in the VGA design.
Pull-up resistors R_DDC_SCL and R_DDC_SDA, 4.7 kohm to +5 V 1.12 mA maximum pull-up current at 5.25 V. PC0 and PC1 are rated to sink 2.4 mA at 0.5 V, so the bus low sits under 0.5 V against a DDC receiver threshold of 1.5 V.
Rise time About 0.4 microseconds at 100 pF of bus capacitance 0.8473 x 4.7 kohm x 100 pF, inside the 1 microsecond standard-mode limit. The same product reaches 1 microsecond near 250 pF.
Bus capacitance About 250 pF with the fitted pull-ups The I2C standard-mode ceiling is 400 pF, but the 4.7 kohm pull-ups reach the 1 microsecond rise limit near 250 pF, so that is the practical cap. A sub-100 kHz firmware-paced clock tolerates a slower edge in any case. Short board routing keeps the routed contribution small; the monitor cable and its EDID EEPROM consume the rest.
Clock rate Set by firmware, below 100 kHz Each bus edge costs at least one PI/T byte access, so the loop cannot approach the standard-mode ceiling. DDC2B sets no minimum clock rate, so a firmware-paced clock is legal at any speed and may pause between bits.

DDC_SCL and DDC_SDA land on J_VGA pins 15 and 12. Pin 9 of that connector carries a fused +5 V supply for the monitor's EDID EEPROM and pin 5 is the DDC ground return; both belong to the VGA design.

Nothing on the motherboard other than the two pull-ups connects to the bus. With no monitor attached, or a monitor with no EDID EEPROM, both lines stay high, which firmware reads as an idle bus.

8. User I/O Header

J_PIT_USER is a 34-pin, 0.1 inch, shrouded and keyed IDC header. It carries 22 signals and interleaves ground pairs between the signal groups so that a ribbon cable has a return next to every group.

The recommended part is the Amphenol ICC 75869-106LF, a 2-by-17 0.1 inch shrouded header with a center polarizing key. Any 2-by-17 shrouded and keyed 0.1 inch header with the same footprint and the pinout below is acceptable.

J_PIT_USER pinout
Pin Signal Pin Signal
1 +5 V fused 2 +5 V fused
3 GND 4 GND
5 PA0 6 PA1
7 PA2 8 PA3
9 PA4 10 PA5
11 PA6 12 PA7
13 GND 14 GND
15 PB0 16 PB1
17 PB2 18 PB3
19 PB4 20 PB5
21 PB6 22 PB7
23 GND 24 GND
25 H1 26 H2
27 H3 28 H4
29 GND 30 GND
31 PC2/TIN 32 PC4
33 GND 34 GND

Pin 1 is marked on copper and silkscreen. The shroud key faces the board edge so a cable cannot seat reversed.

Header Rules

  • The header is unbuffered. Every pin connects to an MC68230 pin through a board trace and nothing else, so attached hardware sees the device's own drive and threshold limits.
  • A port pin programmed as an output sinks 2.4 mA at 0.5 V and sources 150 uA at 2.4 V. The low side drives one standard TTL load or six LS loads; the high side suits CMOS inputs and LS inputs, seven of them at the 20 uA LS figure. An LED, a relay, or anything else with a milliamp-scale high-side draw needs its own driver on the attached board.
  • Attached hardware must not drive a pin that firmware has programmed as an output. The MC68230 port outputs are push-pull.
  • PA7..PA0, PB7..PB0, H2, and H4 hold internal pull-ups, so an unconnected input pin reads high. Those pull-ups source 0.1 to 1.0 mA, so an attached device that pulls one of these pins low must sink 1.0 mA and still hold a valid low.
  • H1 and H3 have no internal pull-up. An attached board drives them or adds its own pull-up.
  • PC2/TIN as an external timer clock is limited to one eighth of PIT_CLK, 1.25 MHz, with the prescaler bypassed, and needs 45 ns in each half period. With the prescaler in use the device accepts up to the CLK frequency itself, but a source unrelated to PIT_CLK should stay at or below 80 percent of it, 8 MHz, or the timer drops cycles. As a run/halt control the low time must last at least one PIT_CLK period.
  • The header carries no reset, no clock, and no bus signal. A card that needs those belongs in an expansion slot.

Header Power

F_PIT_5V, an RXEF050 radial resettable fuse, feeds the +5 V pins of J_PIT_USER. It holds 0.50 A at 20 C and 0.27 A at 70 C, so the header supplies a quarter of an amp at the top of the case temperature range. The expansion slots use larger parts from the same RXEF series.

The header does not supply +12 V. A shorted cable trips F_PIT_5V and leaves the rest of the board running.

9. Timer

The timer is a 24-bit down counter with a 5-bit prescaler. With the clock-control field set to use the CLK pin and the prescaler, the prescaler divides PIT_CLK by 32 and the counter decrements at 312.5 kHz. 

counter tick     = 32 / 10 MHz          = 3.2 us
period           = (preload + 1) x 3.2 us
longest period   = 2^24 x 3.2 us        = 53.687 s
100 Hz preload   = (10 ms / 3.2 us) - 1 = 3124 = $000C34

On zero detect the counter sets the ZDS bit in TSR, asserts TOUT low, and reloads from the preload registers. Reading TSR and writing a one to bit 0 clears the status bit and releases TOUT.

The MFP Timer C already produces the 100 Hz system tick, so firmware owns this timer for measurement, timeouts, and software that wants a second periodic source. The 3.2 microsecond resolution and 53 second range suit interval measurement better than the MFP's 8-bit timers.

PC2/TIN reaches the user header. Firmware that selects the TIN clock source counts external edges instead of the internal clock, and firmware that selects the run/halt source gates the counter from the header. Both choices take PC2 away from port C I/O for as long as they are selected.

10. Interrupts

The PI/T owns two processor levels. Each has its own request pin, its own acknowledge pin, and its own vector register, so the two never need software to work out which source fired.

PI/T interrupt levels
Level Source Request Acknowledge Vector
5 Timer zero detect PC3/TOUT to PIT_TIRQ_n, encoder /I5 IACK_L5_n to PC7/TIACK TIVR, programmed to $54
4 Handshake pins H1 through H4 PC5/PIRQ to PIT_PIRQ_n, encoder /I4 IACK_L4_n to PC6/PIACK PIVR base $50, plus the source number

Both request pins drive low or go to high impedance, so each gets a 4.7 kohm pull-up at the priority encoder: R_PIT_TIRQ and R_PIT_PIRQ. Each pin reaches its new state within 225 ns of the clock edge that caused it, specifications 39 and 44, which the two-stage /IPL synchronizer then samples.

The timer sits above the ports so a periodic source cannot be held off by header activity.

Port Vectors

During a level-4 acknowledge the PI/T replaces the low two bits of PIVR with the number of the highest-priority active handshake source. The mapping is fixed and does not follow the priority field in PSRR.

Port interrupt vector numbers with PIVR set to $50
Source Low two bits Vector number Vector address
H1 00 $50 $000140
H2 01 $51 $000144
H3 10 $52 $000148
H4 11 $53 $00014C

The timer vector $54 lies at $000150. The five PI/T vectors sit above the MFP block at $40-$4F and inside the M68000 user vector range, which starts at 64.

Acknowledge Behavior

An acknowledge cycle places a vector on D7..D0 and asserts PIT_DTACK_n. It changes no register, no data, and no status bit inside the device. 

register cycle:      /CS low,  PIACK high, TIACK high
level-4 acknowledge: /CS high, PIACK low,  TIACK high
level-5 acknowledge: /CS high, PIACK high, TIACK low

The PI/T ignores RS1 through RS5 during an acknowledge cycle. Mask sets GG7 and KD1 carry an erratum in which an acknowledge corrupts PIVR or TIVR if the register selects happen to address one of them. During a CPU-space cycle the processor drives every address line above A3 high and puts the level on A3..A1, so RS5..RS1 read 11100 for level 4 and 11101 for level 5. Both fall in the null block, and neither is the PIVR select 00101 or the TIVR select 10001. The erratum cannot reach this board.

Unanswered Acknowledge Cycles

The PI/T makes no response at all to an acknowledge whose interrupt function is unselected or whose request it is not asserting. It drives no vector and no /DTACK. That happens before firmware programs PSRR and TCR, and after an interrupt is withdrawn between the processor latching the level and running the acknowledge.

The motherboard bus timeout does not run during CPU space, so the phantom acknowledge watchdog terminates those cycles. It fires 3.2 microseconds after an unanswered acknowledge begins, more than six times the PI/T's longest legitimate acknowledge response of under 500 ns. The processor takes the spurious-interrupt exception, vector 24.

PIT_DTACK_n joins MFP_DTACK_n and /AVEC in the watchdog's answered term, so a PI/T acknowledge holds the counter in reset.

11. Firmware Configuration Rules

These rules follow from the board wiring. Register bit fields beyond them belong to the MC68230 data sheet.

  1. Write PCDR bits 1 and 0 to zero before writing PCDDR. Reset leaves the data registers undefined, and a stale one in either bit drives a DDC line high the moment its direction bit is set.
  2. Program the ports in this order: write PGCR bits 7 and 6 to 00 for mode 0 with the H12 and H34 enable bits (5 and 4) clear, set the port A and port B submode fields to the bit I/O submode in PACR and PBCR, choose the handshake sense in PGCR bits 3 through 0, then set the two enable bits. A submode field must not change while its handshake enable is set.
  3. Leave the H12 and H34 enable bits set for as long as the handshake pins are in use. Clearing either one clears the matching status bits in PSR, which withdraws a pending port interrupt.
  4. Set PSRR bits 4 and 3 to 11. That gives PC5 the PIRQ function and PC6 the PIACK function with vectored interrupts. Leave PSRR bit 6 clear so PC4 keeps its port C function and the DMA request stays unselected.
  5. Write PIVR before enabling any handshake interrupt. An unwritten PIVR returns $0F, the M68000 uninitialized-interrupt vector, which is a diagnostic rather than a handler.
  6. Set TCR bits 7 through 5 to 101 for a vectored timer interrupt on PC3/TOUT with PC7 carrying TIACK, and write TIVR before setting the timer enable bit.
  7. Set TCR bits 2 and 1 to 00 to clock the prescaler from the CLK pin and leave PC2 as a port C pin for the header.
  8. Leave TCR bit 4 at zero so the counter reloads from the preload registers on zero detect. That is the periodic mode section 9 describes; reset already clears the bit.
  9. Clear the ZDS bit in TSR inside the level-5 handler by writing a one to bit 0. TOUT stays low and the level stays asserted until that write happens.
  10. Change PSRR bits 2 through 0, the port interrupt priority, only while the affected handshake interrupts are disabled.
  11. Access every register as a byte at an odd address. Read the three count bytes twice when a coherent 24-bit value matters.
  12. Drive the DDC lines by direction only. Set a PCDDR bit to pull its line low and clear it to release the line. Never write a one into PCDR bit 0 or bit 1.

Motherboard Gate

PIT_CS_n uses gate 2 of U_OR_DTACK, the SN74F32N that already carries the timeout mask on gate 1. Input pin 4 takes IO9_n, input pin 5 takes LDS_n, and output pin 6 is PIT_CS_n. Gates 3 and 4 stay unused with their inputs grounded.

Chip Select Arrival

PIT_CS_n follows the slot decode. Bus and Address Decode gives 144 ns from AS_n to any IOx_n through the HCT qualification and slot decoders, and the SN74F32N adds its high-to-low delay. 

AS_n low, from the S2 clock edge     55.0 ns   M68000 #9
AS_n -> IO9_n                       144.0 ns   HCT32, HCT244,
                                               HCT32, HCT138
IO9_n -> PIT_CS_n, SN74F32 tPHL       6.3 ns
--------------------------------------------
PIT_CS_n low, from the S2 clock edge 205.3 ns

A write cycle asserts LDS_n two states later than a read cycle, at S4 rather than S2, but the slot-decode path still arrives last, so both cycle types give the same figure.

The MC68230 samples chip select on a falling clock edge and needs 20 ns of setup. The falling PIT_CLK edge that starts S7 arrives 250 ns after the S2 edge, plus the two buffer stages, so the setup is at least 44.7 ns before counting the buffer delay. The device recognizes the chip select on that edge at the latest.

Cycle Length

The MC68230 asserts /DTACK on the falling clock edge after the one that recognized chip select, within 60 ns of that edge. The processor samples /DTACK on its own falling edges and inserts a wait state whenever the response misses one. 

chip select recognized     falling edge at or before S7
/DTACK asserted            one PIT_CLK period later, plus 60 ns
processor completes        150 ns after the sampling edge that sees it

PI/T byte access           7 to 8 CPU clock periods, 700 to 800 ns

The exact wait-state count moves with the phase between the processor clock and the buffered PI/T clock. Correctness does not depend on the count: a late response adds a wait state, and every count sits inside the 51.1 microsecond timeout. The access length matches the DS1285 interface, which needs 700 to 800 ns for the same reason.

Consecutive PI/T accesses do not reach the 300 ns recovery window. The device asserts /DTACK at least 250 ns before AS_n negates, the processor spends two more clock states before it asserts AS_n again, and the slot decode then takes another 150.3 ns. At least 500 ns separate one /DTACK edge from the next chip select, which also clears the 30 ns minimum select gap of specification 45 by a wide margin.

Acknowledgement Release, Register Cycle

MC68EC000 specification 28 allows 110 ns from strobe negation to /DTACK release. On a register cycle LDS_n rises at the end of S7 and reaches U_OR_DTACK gate 2 with no logic in between, so it, rather than the slow slot decode, releases PIT_CS_n. 

U_OR_DTACK gate 2 SN74F32, tPLH   6.6 ns
MC68230 /CS high to /DTACK high  45.0 ns   PI/T 10
group SN74F21, tPLH               5.3 ns
final SN74F21, tPLH               5.3 ns
SN74F32 timeout mask, tPLH        6.6 ns
------------------------------------------
component total                  68.8 ns
MC68EC000 limit                 110.0 ns
board allowance                  41.2 ns

The device three-states /DTACK within 55 ns of the same edge, specification 11, so it has let go of the net well before the next chip select arrives.

Acknowledgement Release, Acknowledge Cycle

A level-4 or level-5 acknowledge releases through the interrupt decoder, not the chip-select gate. AS_n rises, U_INT_GATE drops IACK_ACTIVE and raises IACK_n, and U_IACK_DEC raises IACK_L4_n or IACK_L5_n. Specification 10 still fixes the 45 ns from that strobe edge to the start of the /DTACK release, but the SN74HCT138 enable-to-output delay, 42 ns from Bus and Address Decode section 24, replaces the 6.6 ns FAST gate of the register path. 

U_IACK_DEC enable to strobe, SN74HCT138  42.0 ns
MC68230 PIACK or TIACK high to /DTACK    45.0 ns   PI/T 10
group SN74F21, tPLH                       5.3 ns
final SN74F21, tPLH                       5.3 ns
SN74F32 timeout mask, tPLH                6.6 ns
----------------------------------------------------
from IACK_n rising                      104.2 ns
MC68EC000 limit, from AS_n negation     110.0 ns

That leaves 5.8 ns of the specification-28 window for the path from AS_n to IACK_n, and the qualifier in U_INT_GATE alone is an SN74HCT08 stage near 30 ns. Summed at the datasheet maxima this page uses everywhere else, the acknowledge release runs past 110 ns with no board allowance, so it is the tightest termination path on the board. The register cycle above is unaffected and keeps its 41.2 ns allowance.

Interrupts section 14 tracks the fix, chosen at schematic capture: bring IACK_n forward with fewer gates, give U_IACK_DEC a FAST or AC part, or route the PI/T a dedicated fast acknowledge strobe. Typical delays at room temperature are far shorter, so the assembled-board measurement decides whether any change is needed.

The MC68901 level-6 acknowledge shares U_IACK_DEC and sees the same decoder delay, so the MFP acknowledge path carries this constraint too.

Acknowledge Cycle

The MC68230 synchronizes PIACK or TIACK on a falling clock edge, drives the vector one clock period later, and asserts /DTACK one clock period after that. That order gives the vector a full 100 ns of setup ahead of its own acknowledgement. 

PIACK/TIACK recognized  falling edge, 40 ns setup   PI/T 31
vector on D7..D0        +1 period, within 100 ns    PI/T 29
/DTACK asserted         +1 period, within 100 ns    PI/T 34

device contribution        under 500 ns worst case
watchdog limit             3.2 us

A missed setup pushes the first synchronizing edge one clock period later, which is where the 500 ns worst case comes from. The response is more than six times faster than the phantom-acknowledge watchdog, so adding two vectored levels does not move the watchdog tap.

Loading

PI/T interface loading
Net Added load Result
A5..A1 One MC68230 register-select input per line 10 uA leakage and 15 pF per line.
D7..D0 One MC68230 data pin per line 20 uA off-state current and 15 pF per line. The pin drives only during a PI/T read or an acknowledge cycle, sourcing 400 uA at 2.4 V and sinking 5.3 mA at 0.5 V.
R/W One MC68230 input 10 uA leakage and 15 pF.
PIT_CLK One MC68230 clock input 10 uA leakage and 15 pF on its own CD74ACT244E channel, leaving 35 pF for routing inside the buffer's 50 pF timing load.
PERIPH_RESET_n One MC68230 reset input 10 uA leakage and 15 pF. Polarity and the 2.0 V TTL threshold match the LS07 open-collector driver.
PIT_DTACK_n 4.7 kohm pull-up and one SN74F21 input 1.12 mA maximum pull-up current at 5.25 V against a 5.3 mA sink rating, 21 percent of it. Off-state current is 20 uA.
PIT_PIRQ_n, PIT_TIRQ_n 4.7 kohm pull-up and one SN74LS148 input each 1.12 mA against the 8.8 mA sink rating that PC5/PIRQ and PC3/TOUT carry, 13 percent of it. These two pins have the strongest low-side drive on the device, which is what the wired-OR role wants.
DDC_SCL, DDC_SDA 4.7 kohm pull-up and one J_VGA DDC pin each 1.12 mA against the 2.4 mA sink rating of PC0 and PC1, 47 percent of it.
IACK_L4_n, IACK_L5_n One MC68230 input each The SN74HCT138 level decoder gains 10 uA and 15 pF per strobe.

Every MC68230 input draws at most 10 uA and presents at most 15 pF, from section 6.4. Add the 15 pF figures to the CPU address, data, and control totals in Bus and Address Decode after routing.

Every pull-up on this page is 4.7 kohm and draws at most 1.12 mA at 5.25 V. The tightest of the three is the DDC pair at 47 percent of the pin's rated sink current, and the device guarantees 0.5 V at the full 2.4 mA, so the actual low sits under that. A DDC receiver reads low below 0.3 times the supply, 1.5 V on this bus, so the level holds with a full volt to spare even at the guaranteed figure.

Internal power dissipation is 750 mW maximum measured at 0 C, which is 150 mA from the +5 V rail. Add that to the board supply budget alongside the user header feed behind F_PIT_5V.

U_PIT gets a 100 nF ceramic bypass capacitor at each supply pin pair and a 1 uF bulk capacitor beside pin 12.

R_PIT_DTACK 4.7 kohm, 0.125 W Completion-tree pull-up.

R_PIT_TIRQ 4.7 kohm, 0.125 W Timer interrupt pull-up.

U_IO_CLK_BUF, the CD74ACT244E that supplies PIT_CLK, belongs to Clock and Reset. PIT_CS_n uses a gate that the motherboard already has. This subsystem adds two 100 nF ceramic bypass capacitors and one 1 uF capacitor beside U_PIT.

U_PIT dissipates at most 750 mW internally, 150 mA from the +5 V rail, before the header draws anything. J_PIT_USER sits behind F_PIT_5V and adds up to 0.27 A more at 70 C.

The archived data sheet is 1983 advance information and lists the plastic 48-pin package with a G suffix, MC68230G10. Production plastic parts carry a P suffix. MC68230P10 is the 10 MHz plastic DIP specified here and in the Memory Map; confirm the suffix against the sourced part. The RXEF series and the CD74ACT244 both predate 1994.

15. Board Layout

  • Place U_PIT so that D7..D0, A5..A1, and R/W reach it without crossing the DRAM or video areas. It is a 48-pin package on a 0.6 inch row spacing and needs the footprint reserved early.
  • Keep PIT_CS_n and PIT_DTACK_n short and free of stubs. Measure the routed register-cycle release path at the CPU /DTACK pin and keep the board contribution below 41.2 ns. The acknowledge-cycle release path in section 13 is tighter and depends on the interrupt-decoder fix.
  • Place R_PIT_DTACK beside U_PIT pin 42. Place R_PIT_PIRQ and R_PIT_TIRQ at the priority encoder, matching the other open-drain interrupt lines.
  • Place R_DDC_SCL and R_DDC_SDA near U_PIT. Route DDC_SCL and DDC_SDA to the J_VGA DDC pins as a short pair away from the clock and video nets; their length counts against the 250 pF bus budget in section 7.
  • Put J_PIT_USER at a board edge that a ribbon cable can reach with the case closed. Mark pin 1 on copper and silkscreen and orient the shroud key away from the board interior.
  • Route F_PIT_5V so that the J_PIT_USER +5 V pins sit behind it and no other load shares the fuse.
  • Include the U_PIT address, data, and control pins in the CPU bus capacitance totals in Bus and Address Decode after routing.
  • Include the PIT_CLK branch in the U_IO_CLK_BUF load check in Clock and Reset. The routed branch must stay inside the CD74ACT244E 50 pF timing-analysis load.
  • Place each 100 nF capacitor at its supply pins and the 1 uF capacitor beside U_PIT pins 12 and 38.
  • Measure PIT_CLK at pin 40 on the assembled board. Confirm a clean 10 MHz edge and confirm the clock runs before reset releases.
